chapters.title: The Body at a Glance
chapters.tease: Outside you look symmetrical; inside, the liver leans right, the stomach left, and the heart sits almost centre.

chapters.title: Thirty-Seven Trillion Cells
chapters.tease: Five in every six of your cells are red blood cells, and not one of them carries any DNA.

chapters.title: Inside a Cell
chapters.tease: Each cell runs a power plant, a factory, a post office and a recycling centre, all too small to see.

chapters.title: DNA: The Instruction Manual
chapters.tease: Each nucleus packs about two metres of DNA into a space roughly six thousandths of a millimetre wide.

chapters.title: Proteins: The Body's Workers
chapters.tease: Four letters of DNA, read three at a time, are enough to build every enzyme, hormone and fibre in your body.

chapters.title: Stem Cells
chapters.tease: Your bone marrow makes about two million new red blood cells every second, from a small reserve of stem cells.

chapters.title: Four Kinds of Tissue
chapters.tease: Lip, liver and tendon look nothing alike, yet all are woven from the same four kinds of tissue.

chapters.title: Organs and Systems
chapters.tease: An organ is just tissues cooperating; a system is organs sharing a job, and none of them works alone.

chapters.title: What We Are Made Of
chapters.tease: By weight you are mostly oxygen; by headcount of atoms you are mostly hydrogen, forged in the Big Bang.

chapters.title: Homeostasis: Keeping in Balance
chapters.tease: Frost or heatwave, your core stays within about a degree of 37 °C, thanks to a thermostat the size of an almond.

chapters.title: The Skeleton
chapters.tease: More than half of your 206 bones are in your hands and feet: 106 of them.

chapters.title: Inside a Bone
chapters.tease: Your skeleton is rebuilt about once a decade: cells dissolve and relay roughly a tenth of it every year.

chapters.title: The Skull
chapters.tease: A newborn's skull is still in loose pieces, with soft spots that let it squeeze through the birth canal.

chapters.title: The Spine
chapters.tease: You are about a centimetre shorter at bedtime than at breakfast, because your spinal discs squeeze out water.

chapters.title: Joints
chapters.tease: The cartilage in a healthy joint slides with less friction than ice on ice, and it has no blood supply at all.

chapters.title: The Hand
chapters.tease: Your fingers contain no muscles at all. They are worked like puppets by tendons from the forearm.

chapters.title: Feet and Walking Upright
chapters.tease: With every step your foot turns from a soft shock absorber into a rigid lever, then back again.

chapters.title: How Muscles Contract
chapters.tease: When a muscle contracts, nothing inside it gets shorter. Billions of tiny protein heads pull filaments past each other.

chapters.title: Tendons and Ligaments
chapters.tease: Your Achilles tendon works like a spring, storing energy as your foot lands and giving it back as you push off.

chapters.title: Strength, Speed and Stamina
chapters.tease: A muscle holds only a couple of seconds' worth of fuel, yet the body recycles about its own weight in ATP each day.

chapters.title: The Heart
chapters.tease: A fist-sized muscle that beats about 100,000 times a day and never takes a day off.

chapters.title: The Heartbeat
chapters.tease: Every beat starts with a rice-grain of tissue that fires on its own, with no orders from the brain.

chapters.title: Arteries, Veins and Capillaries
chapters.tease: Laid end to end, your blood vessels are often said to reach around 100,000 kilometres.

chapters.title: Blood
chapters.tease: Spin a tube of blood and it separates like a cocktail: straw-coloured plasma above, red cells below.

chapters.title: Red Blood Cells
chapters.tease: Twenty-five trillion tiny discs, each with no nucleus, carrying a billion oxygen molecules apiece.

chapters.title: Blood Groups
chapters.tease: Four letters and a plus or minus decide whose blood can safely save your life.

chapters.title: Clotting
chapters.tease: A cascade of a dozen proteins turns liquid blood into a solid seal, but only where it is needed.

chapters.title: Blood Pressure
chapters.tease: The first reading was taken from a horse in 1733: its blood rose two and a half metres up a glass tube.

chapters.title: The Lymphatic System
chapters.tease: Every day about three litres of fluid leak from your blood; a second network quietly brings it home.

chapters.title: The Kidneys
chapters.tease: Two fist-sized beans filter about 180 litres of fluid a day and hand back all but a litre or two.

chapters.title: The Airways
chapters.tease: Every breath is heated to 37°C and soaked with water vapour before it gets anywhere near a lung.

chapters.title: The Lungs
chapters.tease: Your windpipe splits in two about 23 times in a row, ending in millions of air sacs.

chapters.title: Alveoli: Where Air Meets Blood
chapters.tease: The surface where air meets blood covers about 70 square metres, yet is only half a micrometre thick.

chapters.title: The Diaphragm and Breathing
chapters.tease: Breathing in is hard work; at rest, breathing out is just the lungs springing back.

chapters.title: Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide
chapters.tease: Oxygen moves through you by sliding down a slope of pressure, from 160 in the air to a few in a cell.

chapters.title: The Voice
chapters.tease: Every word you speak is breath chopped into puffs by two small folds, a hundred or more times a second.

chapters.title: Coughs, Sneezes and Yawns
chapters.tease: A cough, a sneeze and a yawn all run the same breathing script, taken out of your hands by the brainstem.

chapters.title: Breathing at Altitude
chapters.tease: At the top of Everest the air is still 21% oxygen. What it lacks is pressure to push it into your blood.

chapters.title: Holding Your Breath
chapters.tease: The urge that ends a breath-hold comes from rising carbon dioxide, not from running out of oxygen.

chapters.title: Breathing During Exercise
chapters.tease: Hard exercise can raise the air you breathe from 6 litres a minute to more than 100.

chapters.title: Teeth and Chewing
chapters.tease: Enamel is the hardest substance in the body, and it is the one tissue that can never repair itself.

chapters.title: Swallowing
chapters.tease: Food and air share one crossroads in the throat, and a reflex lasting under a second keeps them apart.

chapters.title: The Stomach
chapters.tease: Your stomach makes acid strong enough to kill most microbes, and renews its own lining every few days to survive it.

chapters.title: The Small Intestine
chapters.tease: A tube 2.5 cm wide hides an absorbing surface of around 30 square metres, built from folds on folds on folds.

chapters.title: The Liver
chapters.tease: One kind of cell runs hundreds of jobs, and the organ can regrow from a quarter of its mass.

chapters.title: The Pancreas and Blood Sugar
chapters.tease: Two hormones from cell clusters smaller than a grain of sand keep your blood sugar in a narrow band all day.

chapters.title: The Large Intestine
chapters.tease: The colon takes in about a litre and a half of fluid a day and sends out only a cupful.

chapters.title: The Gut Microbiome
chapters.tease: Your colon holds one of the densest microbial crowds on Earth, about as many bacteria as you have cells.

chapters.title: Metabolism: Burning Fuel
chapters.tease: Every cell burns its fuel with oxygen, and an adult recycles roughly their own weight in ATP every day.

chapters.title: Vitamins and Minerals
chapters.tease: A few milligrams a day decide whether bones harden, blood carries oxygen and wounds knit, as sailors learned.

chapters.title: The Brain
chapters.tease: Three pounds of tissue with 86 billion neurons, running on about the power of a dim light bulb.

chapters.title: Neurons
chapters.tease: A single neuron can be a metre long, and its signal can travel at about 120 metres a second.

chapters.title: Synapses and Neurotransmitters
chapters.tease: Neurons never quite touch: every message crosses a gap about 30 millionths of a millimetre wide.

chapters.title: The Spinal Cord and Reflexes
chapters.tease: A finger-thick cable 45 cm long that can make you kick before your brain hears about it.

chapters.title: The Autonomic Nervous System
chapters.tease: Two branches of nerves run your heart, gut and pupils without you ever thinking about them.

chapters.title: Memory
chapters.tease: You do not replay memories, you rebuild them, a little differently each time.

chapters.title: Learning and Plasticity
chapters.tease: A toddler has far more synapses than an adult; growing up is partly a matter of cutting them back.

chapters.title: Emotions
chapters.tease: Your amygdala can make you jump back from a hosepipe before you know it is not a snake.

chapters.title: Sleep
chapters.tease: Every 90 minutes through the night you sink into deep sleep and rise again into dreaming.

chapters.title: Consciousness
chapters.tease: You can be awake without being aware, and aware without being able to move a muscle.

chapters.title: The Eye
chapters.tease: A 24-millimetre ball that focuses an upside-down image onto a sheet thinner than a credit card.

chapters.title: How We See Colour
chapters.tease: Three kinds of cone and a lot of comparison let most of us tell apart perhaps a million shades.

chapters.title: The Ear
chapters.tease: The smallest bone in the body is a 3-millimetre stirrup that helps turn air waves into nerve signals.

chapters.title: Balance
chapters.tease: Three fluid-filled loops and a scattering of tiny stones keep the world steady every time you move your head.

chapters.title: Smell
chapters.tease: About 400 kinds of receptor play chords that the brain reads as smells, wiring straight to memory and emotion.

chapters.title: Taste
chapters.tease: Every part of the tongue tastes all five tastes, and much of what we call flavour is really smell.

chapters.title: Touch
chapters.tease: Your fingertips pack around 240 touch units into each square centimetre, each tuned to a different kind of contact.

chapters.title: Pain
chapters.tease: A stubbed toe sends two alarms: a sharp jab in a fraction of a second and a dull ache a moment later.

chapters.title: Proprioception: The Sixth Sense
chapters.tease: Close your eyes and touch your nose: a hidden sense tracks every limb, many times a second.

chapters.title: Illusions: When Senses Disagree
chapters.tease: Perception is the brain's best guess, and illusions are the moments when the guess and the world come apart.

chapters.title: The Skin
chapters.tease: Your largest organ weighs about 4 kilograms, and you wear a completely new surface of it every month.

chapters.title: Hair and Nails
chapters.tease: Everything you can see of a hair or a nail is dead; only the hidden roots are alive.

chapters.title: Wound Healing
chapters.tease: A cut runs a four-stage repair programme that starts in seconds and is still working a year later.

chapters.title: Inflammation and Fever
chapters.tease: Redness, heat, swelling and pain are not damage: they are the body's repair crew arriving.

chapters.title: Innate Immunity
chapters.tease: Before any antibody is made, five layers of inborn defence stop almost every germ that tries to get in.

chapters.title: White Blood Cells
chapters.tease: One stem cell in the bone marrow gives rise to a whole army of specialist defenders.

chapters.title: Antibodies
chapters.tease: A Y-shaped protein 10 nanometres across, and your body can make billions of different versions.

chapters.title: Vaccines and Immune Memory
chapters.tease: The immune system remembers: a second meeting with a germ is faster, bigger and often silent.

chapters.title: Allergies and Autoimmunity
chapters.tease: Allergy attacks the harmless; autoimmunity attacks the self. Both are a capable immune system aiming wrongly.

chapters.title: Fighting Cancer
chapters.tease: Your immune system kills would-be cancer cells every day; tumours are the ones that learned to hide.

chapters.title: The Endocrine System
chapters.tease: Dozens of hormones steer growth, mood and metabolism, all directed from a control centre the size of an almond.

chapters.title: Adrenaline and Stress
chapters.tease: Adrenaline can double your heart rate within seconds, before you have consciously noticed the danger.

chapters.title: The Thyroid and Growth
chapters.tease: A 20-gram butterfly in your neck decides how fast nearly every cell in your body burns its fuel.

chapters.title: The Body Clock
chapters.tease: Your brain keeps a clock that runs slightly slow, about 24 hours 10 minutes, and morning light resets it every day.

chapters.title: Reproduction
chapters.tease: A girl is born with all the eggs she will ever have; a man makes around 1,500 new sperm every second.

chapters.title: Conception
chapters.tease: Of the tens of millions of sperm released, only a few hundred reach the egg, and just one gets in.

chapters.title: The Embryo
chapters.tease: In week three you were a disc of three cell layers smaller than a grain of rice, and every organ grew from one of them.

chapters.title: Pregnancy
chapters.tease: In 40 weeks a single cell becomes a baby of about 3.4 kilograms, fed by an organ grown for the purpose.

chapters.title: Birth
chapters.tease: Labour runs on positive feedback, one of the few body systems built to escalate rather than calm itself down.

chapters.title: Inheritance: Why We Look Like Our Parents
chapters.tease: Each parent can make about 8.4 million different chromosome combinations, before crossing over shuffles them further.

chapters.title: Babies and Infancy
chapters.tease: A newborn rewires its own heart within minutes of birth, closing a flap it used for nine months.

chapters.title: Childhood and Growth
chapters.tease: By about the age of two, a child is already roughly half as tall as they will ever be.

chapters.title: Puberty
chapters.tease: Puberty starts not in the body but in an almond-sized patch of brain that begins to pulse at night.

chapters.title: The Adult Body
chapters.tease: You get a new gut lining every few days and a new skeleton every decade, but the core of each lens is as old as you.

chapters.title: Ageing
chapters.tease: From about 30, every organ quietly loses a little reserve each year, long before anyone notices.

chapters.title: Exercise and Fitness
chapters.tease: A trained heart pumps about 100 millilitres a beat, so it can rest at 50 beats a minute or fewer.

chapters.title: Nutrition and Health
chapters.tease: A gram of fat carries about 9 kilocalories, more than twice the energy in the same weight of sugar.

chapters.title: Transplants and Spare Parts
chapters.tease: The first lasting organ transplant worked because donor and patient were identical twins.

chapters.title: Medical Imaging: Seeing Inside
chapters.tease: The first X-ray of a hand was taken within weeks of the rays' discovery in 1895.

chapters.title: The Future Body
chapters.tease: In 2023 a treatment that edits a patient's own DNA was approved for the first time.
